A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures and complete appendices support comparison; v2 retains Appendices A–E and adds Appendix F.

before.justification: Section 1 reports GPT-5 mini returning 'Colosseum' for the five-example chess-opening prompt in Figure 2. This is a small original qualitative observation, although the regression contribution is theoretical.

after.justification: Besides retaining the chess-prompt observation, Section 5 and Figure 7 report original regression simulations comparing a trained transformer with a local cubic estimator.

M1.justification: The principal linear-attention estimator and local-polynomial construction remain unchanged. The auxiliary softmax adaptation changes from an affine-rescaling argument to two softmax attention layers followed by O(log n) corrective FFN layers per linear layer, with an expanded intermediate representation in Appendix F.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on synthetic regression tasks generated using random Fourier series, with d=3, alpha=3 and noise scale sigma=0.01. v1 treats regression theoretically and reports only the illustrative chess-prompt outcome.

E2.justification: Section 5 introduces an empirical comparison against a ridge-regularized local cubic estimator. In v1, local polynomial estimation is a theoretical reference rather than an evaluated baseline. Kim et al. and Shen et al. remain literature comparisons, not experimentally evaluated methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a full regression evaluation protocol: a 12-block transformer with embedding dimension 256 and FFN width 1024, 50,000 AdamW steps with 640 sequences per step, and 100,000 test tasks for each n in {15,20,25,30,35}. Baseline bandwidth and ridge penalty are selected by five-fold cross-validation. These are new experiments, not revisions to matching v1 experiments.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds a limited analysis of context-length dependence, examining how both estimators' excess risks vary across five values of n. No component ablations, distribution-shift tests or additional error analyses are introduced; the chess example is retained.

E5.justification: Figure 7 newly reports 90% confidence intervals for excess population risks based on 100,000 test sequences. v1 has no comparable empirical uncertainty reporting. These intervals do not establish repeated transformer training runs, and no training-seed information is supplied.

E6.justification: Figure 7 adds regression results showing lower excess risk for the transformer than the local cubic estimator at all five tested context lengths, with both risks decreasing as n increases. v1 has no corresponding regression scores for a before-and-after performance comparison. The reported chess-prompt response is unchanged.

T1.justification: v1's Section 3 incorrectly gives the softmax derivative as (d−1)x_j/d² and uses it to claim an affine approximation to the identity. Appendix F replaces this with the mean-centered derivative x_j/n−sum_i(x_i)/n² and a constructive attention-plus-FFN derivation. Section 3 consequently specifies Θ(log² n) layers for the softmax extension. The main linear-attention theorems and mathematics in Appendices A–E remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement and summary retain the central claims: minimax-optimal nonparametric regression for every alpha>0 using Θ(log n) transformer parameters and the same pretraining-sequence bound. The added simulations do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: The applicability discussion now explicitly qualifies the softmax extension as requiring Θ(log² n) layers, replacing v1's unqualified statement that similar results follow from an affine softmax approximation. The added optimization caveat in Section 2.4 largely repeats the limitation already stated in v1's Section 3.

D1.justification: Section 5 adds simulation implementation details, including architecture, optimizer, weight decay, learning-rate schedule, batching and baseline tuning grids. It also reports an 80 GB NVIDIA A100, approximately 2.25 hours of pretraining, and a simulation-code link. v1 contains no corresponding experimental implementation or access information.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bhatia (1997) and Kallenberg (2021) as sources for Weyl's inequality and the Doob–Dynkin lemma. The positioning against Kim et al. and Shen et al. is unchanged. The updated Ma et al. title and duplicated AdamW bibliography entry do not represent additional distinct works.

P1.justification: v2 adds explanatory paragraphs about the data-generating setup, optimization and proof strategy, inserts a Simulations section before the Summary, and adds acknowledgements, an impact statement and Appendix F. Most existing prose and section order are retained, with limited terminology and title-style edits.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with new typography, running headers and resized or repositioned Figures 1–6. Figure 7 adds an excess-risk plot with legends and confidence intervals. The appendices remain single-column.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the softmax extension by replacing an erroneous expansion with a constructive argument and an explicit depth cost. Its documented regression comparison and confidence intervals also add useful empirical support. The overall gain is limited: the central linear-attention theory is unchanged, and the single synthetic setting with a fixed architecture does not directly test the headline parameter or pretraining-sample scaling claims.
